questions.content:
Karvala is a rapidly growing coastal city in a middle-income country. Most newcomers arrive from rural villages in the interior.

Karvala: total population
Year: 1990 | 2000 | 2010 | 2020
Population (millions): 2.1 | 4.0 | 7.2 | 11.4

(a) Calculate the increase in Karvala's population between 2000 and 2020. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in population between 2010 and 2020. Show your working and give your answer to one decimal place. (2 marks)
(c) State two push factors that might cause people to leave rural villages for Karvala. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 11.4 - 4.0 = 7.4 million (accept 7,400,000).
[1] (b) Correct working: (11.4 - 7.2) / 7.2 x 100.
[1] (b) Answer 58.3% (accept 58%).
[1] (c) First valid push factor, e.g. lack of jobs, low farm incomes, poor services, drought or crop failure.
[1] (c) Second different valid push factor.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
A student group investigated how a river changes between its source and mouth. They measured four sites on the River Tamsin.

Site: distance from source (km) | channel width (m) | average depth (m) | average velocity (m/s)
Site 1: 0 | 2 | 0.2 | 0.3
Site 2: 5 | 6 | 0.5 | 0.5
Site 3: 12 | 11 | 0.9 | 0.8
Site 4: 20 | 18 | 1.3 | 1.1

(a) Describe how channel width changes with distance from the source. (2 marks)
(b) Assume the channel at Site 3 is a rectangle. Calculate the discharge (in cubic metres per second) at Site 3 using: discharge = cross-sectional area x velocity. Show each step of your working. (3 marks)
(c) Suggest one limitation of measuring velocity at only one point in the channel. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) General trend: width increases downstream / further from the source.
[1] (a) Supporting data, e.g. from 2 m at Site 1 to 18 m at Site 4 (accept an increasing rate of change).
[1] (b) Cross-sectional area = width x depth = 11 x 0.9 = 9.9 square metres.
[1] (b) Discharge = area x velocity = 9.9 x 0.8.
[1] (b) Answer 7.92 cubic metres per second (accept 7.9 or 8 if working shown).
[1] (c) Velocity varies across the channel (faster in the centre, slower near the banks and bed), so one reading may not be representative / may give an inaccurate average.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Two earthquakes of the same magnitude (7.0) struck densely populated coastal areas in different countries.

Event | Location | Deaths | People injured | Buildings destroyed
Event X | Kestrel Bay (high-income country) | 12 | 420 | 2,000
Event Y | Dunmara (low-income country) | 1,850 | 9,600 | 38,000

Both earthquakes happened near a convergent plate boundary where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate.

(a) Explain how movement at a convergent plate boundary can cause an earthquake. (3 marks)
(b) Use the data to compare the impacts of the two earthquakes. (2 marks)
(c) Suggest one reason why Event Y caused more damage than Event X. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) The plates move towards each other / one is forced beneath the other (subduction).
[1] (a) Friction stops the plates sliding, so pressure / strain builds up over time.
[1] (a) When the pressure exceeds the friction the plates suddenly slip, releasing energy as seismic waves that shake the ground.
[1] (b) Event Y had far more deaths than Event X, with figures, e.g. 1,850 compared with 12.
[1] (b) Event Y had more injuries and more destroyed buildings (9,600 and 38,000 compared with 420 and 2,000), or a calculated comparison such as about 19 times as many buildings destroyed.
[1] (c) A valid reason, e.g. weaker building standards, poorer emergency services, less money for preparation or earthquake-proof design, lower levels of education and drills.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Three countries reported their carbon dioxide emissions per person (tonnes per year).

Country | 2000 | 2020
Country P | 3.0 | 4.5
Country Q | 10.0 | 8.0
Country R | 1.5 | 3.0

Use clear geographical terms in your answers.

(a) Calculate the percentage change in emissions per person for Country Q and for Country R between 2000 and 2020. (2 marks)
(b) Describe two ways a country could reduce greenhouse gas emissions (mitigation). (2 marks)
(c) Explain one way a low-lying coastal community could adapt to rising sea levels. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Country Q: -20% (a decrease of 20%).
[1] (a) Country R: +100% (an increase of 100%, emissions doubled).
[1] (b) First valid mitigation method, e.g. switching to renewable energy, improving public transport, planting trees, carbon taxes.
[1] (b) Second different valid mitigation method.
[1] (c) Identifies a valid adaptation, e.g. building sea walls or mangrove barriers, raising homes on stilts, early warning systems, relocating settlements.
[1] (c) Explains how it helps, e.g. the wall stops waves flooding homes, so damage and loss of life are reduced.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
The country of Norvia has an ageing population. The table shows its age structure.

Age group | 1980 (% of population) | 2020 (% of population)
0 - 14 years | 28 | 15
15 - 64 years | 64 | 62
65 years and over | 8 | 23

The dependency ratio = (percentage aged 0 - 14 + percentage aged 65 and over) divided by (percentage aged 15 - 64), multiplied by 100.

(a) Calculate the dependency ratio for Norvia in 2020. Show your working. (2 marks)
(b) Describe the change in the share of the population aged 65 and over between 1980 and 2020. (1 mark)
(c) Explain two problems an ageing population can cause for a government. (2 marks)
(d) Suggest one policy Norvia could introduce to respond to an ageing population. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Working: (15 + 23) / 62 x 100.
[1] (a) Answer 61.3 (accept 61).
[1] (b) The share rose from 8% to 23%, an increase of 15 percentage points (accept nearly tripled).
[1] (c) First problem with development, e.g. higher spending on pensions and healthcare, but fewer workers paying taxes.
[1] (c) Second different problem with development, e.g. labour shortages slow the economy, or care homes and services become overstretched.
[1] (d) A valid policy, e.g. raising the retirement age, encouraging immigration of young workers, offering incentives to have children.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
The table shows development indicators for four countries.

Country | GNI per capita (US dollars) | Life expectancy (years) | Adult literacy rate (%)
Country A | 42,000 | 82 | 99
Country B | 9,500 | 74 | 94
Country C | 1,800 | 62 | 58
Country D | 31,000 | 68 | 78

In Country D, the richest 10% of the population receive 55% of the national income. Most of its wealth comes from oil exports.

(a) Calculate how many times greater the GNI per capita of Country A is than that of Country C. Give your answer to one decimal place. (2 marks)
(b) Identify one development indicator, not shown in the table, that could be used to measure development. (1 mark)
(c) Analyse why GNI per capita alone can be a misleading measure of development. Use Country D in your answer. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Working: 42,000 / 1,800.
[1] (a) Answer 23.3.
[1] (b) A valid indicator, e.g. infant mortality rate, access to clean water, Human Development Index, years of schooling, number of doctors per 1,000 people.
[1] (c) GNI per capita is an average, which hides inequality in how income is shared.
[1] (c) Country D has a high GNI per capita (31,000) but the richest 10% receive 55% of income, so most people may be much poorer than the average suggests.
[1] (c) Country D's life expectancy (68) and literacy (78%) are lower than Country B despite a much higher GNI, showing income does not guarantee good health or education.
[1] (c) Development also includes social and environmental factors (health, education, freedom, sustainability) that GNI does not measure, so several indicators should be combined.
Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Brightmoor is a city of 3.2 million people. Traffic congestion is severe and the average commute is 62 minutes. The city council must choose between two projects but can afford only one.

Option 1: Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) network
Cost: 1.2 billion dollars
Average commute after completion: 41 minutes
Change in transport carbon dioxide emissions: -18%
Jobs created: 3,000
Households displaced: 1,200

Option 2: New ring road
Cost: 0.9 billion dollars
Average commute after completion: 52 minutes
Change in transport carbon dioxide emissions: +9%
Jobs created: 1,500
Households displaced: 3,400
Farmland lost: 410 hectares

Evaluate which option would contribute more to the sustainable development of Brightmoor. Support your answer with evidence from the data and reach a justified conclusion. (9 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Option 1 social benefit with data: commute falls by 21 minutes (about 34%), a bigger gain than the ring road.
[1] Option 1 environmental benefit: emissions fall by 18%, supporting sustainability / helping tackle climate change and air pollution.
[1] Option 1 economic benefit: creates 3,000 jobs (twice as many as the ring road) and more people can reach work reliably.
[1] Option 2 benefit with data: lower cost (0.9 billion compared with 1.2 billion, a saving of 0.3 billion) and it still cuts the commute by 10 minutes (about 16%).
[1] Option 2 environmental harm: emissions rise by 9% and 410 hectares of farmland is lost, which is not sustainable for future generations.
[1] Option 2 social harm: 3,400 households displaced, almost three times as many as Option 1, causing loss of homes and communities.
[1] Option 1 drawback / limitation: higher cost and 1,200 households still displaced, so the council needs compensation, funding and fair rehousing.
[1] Evaluative weighing of the criteria: sustainability involves balancing economic, social and environmental needs, and the ring road's lower cost is a short-term gain against long-term harm (or equivalent judgement).
[1] Clear conclusion that is consistent with the evidence, e.g. the BRT is the more sustainable option, with a justification and, for full credit, a recognition of one condition or uncertainty (e.g. whether people will actually use the buses).
Accept other valid points.
